decks.title: Cell: The Unit of Life — Part 1: Cell theory, cell types, membrane and wall
goals: State the cell theory and the contributions that built it
Describe the fluid mosaic model and transport across membranes
Describe the plant cell wall and middle lamella

slides.heading: Cell: The Unit of Life
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how we learnt that all life is made of cells, and how the simplest cells and the cell boundary are built.

visual.alt: Flow of discoveries leading to the cell theory

slides.narration: Anything less than a complete cell cannot live independently, so the cell is the fundamental unit of life. Unicellular organisms carry out all life processes within one cell, while multicellular organisms are built of many cells.

slides.heading: The cell theory
slides.body_md: The cell theory grew from the work of several scientists.

rows: First saw and described a live cell
Plants are made of different kinds of cells forming tissues
Animal cells have a thin outer layer (plasma membrane); the cell wall is unique to plant cells; bodies are made of cells and their products
New cells arise from pre-existing cells

visual.alt: Table of scientists and their contributions to the cell theory

slides.narration: Schleiden and Schwann together proposed that plants and animals are composed of cells and products of cells, but they could not explain how new cells formed. Virchow showed that cells divide, so every cell comes from a pre-existing cell. These two ideas make up the modern cell theory.

slides.heading: Sizes and shapes of cells
slides.body_md: Cells vary greatly in size and shape, which suits their functions.

visual.alt: Table of cell sizes from Mycoplasma to the ostrich egg

slides.narration: Cells may be disc-like, polygonal, columnar, cuboidal, thread-like or irregular. A red blood cell is a flexible disc that slips through capillaries, while a nerve cell is long enough to carry messages across the body.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: finding a magnification
slides.body_md: A bacterium 3 µm long appears 18 mm long in an electron micrograph. What is the magnification?
bullets: Magnification $= \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{real size}}$, with both in the same unit.
An image like this could only come from an electron microscope; light microscopes magnify much less.

visual.alt: Worked table: magnification 6000

slides.narration: First convert eighteen millimetres to eighteen thousand micrometres. Then divide by the real length of three micrometres. The magnification is six thousand times.

slides.heading: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
slides.body_md: Cells are of two kinds, depending on whether the genetic material is enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

rows: Present: ER, Golgi, mitochondria and others

visual.alt: Table comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

slides.narration: Prokaryotes have no nuclear envelope and no membrane-bound organelles, only ribosomes. Eukaryotic cells are divided into many compartments by membranes. Among eukaryotes, plant cells have walls, plastids and a large central vacuole, while animal cells have centrioles.

slides.heading: A prokaryotic cell
slides.body_md: Bacteria may be rods (**bacillus**), spheres (**coccus**), commas (**vibrio**) or spirals (**spirillum**). The genomic DNA is a single circular chromosome; **plasmids** carry extra genes such as antibiotic resistance.

slides.narration: The cell envelope has three layers: the glycocalyx outside, then the cell wall, then the plasma membrane. The mesosome, an infolding of the membrane, helps in forming the wall, copying and sharing DNA, respiration and secretion. Flagella give motility, while pili and fimbriae help in attachment.

slides.heading: The bacterial cell envelope and inclusions
slides.body_md: Differences in the envelope explain why some bacteria are **Gram-positive** (take up the Gram stain) and others **Gram-negative**.

rows: Loose sheath: slime layer; thick and tough: capsule
Fixes shape, stops bursting or collapse
70S (50S plus 30S), about 15 nm by 20 nm; may form polysomes on one mRNA
Phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules, not membrane-bound; gas vacuoles in some photosynthetic bacteria

visual.alt: Table of the bacterial envelope, ribosomes and inclusions

slides.narration: The envelope works as a single protective unit. Ribosomes, attached to the plasma membrane, make proteins, and several may work along one messenger RNA as a polysome. Reserve foods lie free in the cytoplasm as inclusion bodies.

slides.heading: The plasma membrane
slides.body_md: Studies on human red blood cells show a **lipid bilayer**, mainly of phosphoglycerides, with **polar heads outwards** and **hydrophobic tails inwards**. The red cell membrane has about **52 percent protein** and **40 percent lipid**.

slides.narration: In the fluid mosaic model of Singer and Nicolson, the lipid is quasi-fluid, so proteins can move sideways. Integral proteins are partly or totally buried, and peripheral proteins lie on the surface. Fluidity is needed for growth, cell junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

slides.heading: Transport across the membrane
slides.body_md: The membrane is **selectively permeable**.

rows: Neutral solutes move down their concentration gradient
Polar molecules cross the non-polar bilayer with carrier proteins
Ions such as sodium moved against the gradient, as by the sodium–potassium pump

visual.alt: Table of passive and active transport across the membrane

slides.narration: Passive transport moves substances from high to low concentration without spending energy. Polar molecules cannot dissolve through the lipid core, so they need carrier proteins. Active transport pumps substances against the gradient and uses energy from ATP.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which kind of transport?
slides.body_md: Decide how each substance crosses the membrane.
bullets: Carbon dioxide leaving a respiring cell, where it is more concentrated inside → **simple diffusion**.
Water entering a dried raisin placed in water → **osmosis**.
Glucose, a polar molecule, entering a cell down its gradient → **carrier protein** (passive).
Potassium taken into a cell that already has more potassium than the outside → **active transport** with ATP.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four movements across the membrane

slides.narration: Ask two questions. Is the substance moving down or against its gradient? And can it pass through lipid? Down the gradient through lipid is diffusion; water is osmosis; polar molecules need carriers; anything against the gradient needs energy.

slides.body_md: How are the lipid molecules arranged in the membrane?
slides.narration: Quick check. Which part of the lipid avoids water?

slides.heading: The cell wall
slides.body_md: Fungi and plants have a **non-living rigid cell wall** outside the plasma membrane. It gives shape, protects against mechanical damage and infection, helps cell-to-cell interaction and blocks undesirable macromolecules.

rows: Cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals such as calcium carbonate
Thin wall of young cells, capable of growth
Formed on the inner side, towards the membrane, as the cell matures
Mainly calcium pectate; glues neighbouring cells
Cross the wall and middle lamella, connecting neighbouring cytoplasms

visual.alt: Table of cell wall composition and layers

slides.narration: The primary wall can grow, but its capacity falls as the cell matures, and a secondary wall is laid down inside it. Neighbouring cells are glued by the middle lamella and linked by fine cytoplasmic strands called plasmodesmata.

slides.heading: Quick check: middle lamella
slides.body_md: What is the main substance of the middle lamella?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is a calcium compound.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Cell theory: organisms are made of cells and cell products; cells arise from pre-existing cells (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow).
Sizes: Mycoplasma 0.3 µm, bacteria 3 to 5 µm, red cell 7 µm; ostrich egg largest single cell.
Prokaryotes: no nuclear envelope, no membrane-bound organelles; envelope of glycocalyx, wall and membrane; mesosomes, plasmids, 70S ribosomes, inclusion bodies, flagella, pili, fimbriae.
Fluid mosaic membrane: lipid bilayer with integral and peripheral proteins; passive and active transport.
Cell wall: primary and secondary walls, middle lamella of calcium pectate, plasmodesmata.

visual.alt: Summary table of four key ideas

slides.narration: To recap: the cell is the unit of life, and every cell comes from another. Prokaryotes lack a nuclear envelope and membrane organelles. The plasma membrane is a fluid bilayer that controls transport, and plant cells add a rigid wall outside it.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State **both parts** of the cell theory and credit **Virchow**.
Compare prokaryotes and eukaryotes in a **table** of three or more features.
Draw the **fluid mosaic** membrane with labels.
Classify transport by **gradient** and **energy**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write both statements of the cell theory. Use tables to compare cell types. Practise a labelled drawing of the fluid mosaic membrane. And always decide transport type from the gradient and the need for energy.

slides.narration: Many membrane-bound organelles work together as the endomembrane system: the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included, because their functions are not coordinated with these.

slides.heading: An animal cell
slides.body_md: Animal cells have **centrioles** and lack a cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole.

slides.narration: In a mature plant cell the central vacuole, bounded by the tonoplast, may fill up to ninety percent of the cell and pushes the nucleus and cytoplasm to the edges. Chloroplasts trap light, and plasmodesmata cross the wall to link neighbouring cells.

slides.heading: Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus
slides.body_md: The **ER** is a network of tubules that divides the cell into a **luminal** (inside ER) and an **extra-luminal** (cytoplasm) compartment. The **Golgi apparatus**, seen by **Camillo Golgi (1898)**, is a stack of flat cisternae 0.5 to 1.0 µm across.

rows: Ribosomes on outer surface; continuous with nuclear envelope
Lipid synthesis; steroid hormones in animal cells
Cisternae with convex cis (forming) face and concave trans (maturing) face
Modifies and packages materials; forms glycoproteins and glycolipids

visual.alt: Table of rough ER, smooth ER and Golgi apparatus

slides.narration: Vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus. Inside the cisternae the proteins are modified and packaged, and they leave from the trans face, either for use inside the cell or for secretion.

slides.heading: Lysosomes, vacuoles and microbodies
slides.body_md: Three more kinds of membrane-bound sacs.

rows: Formed by Golgi packaging; hydrolytic enzymes (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) active at acidic pH; digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids
Bounded by the tonoplast; water, sap, excretory products; up to 90 percent of a plant cell; tonoplast moves ions in against their gradient
Minute vesicles with enzymes, in plant and animal cells

visual.alt: Table of lysosomes, vacuoles and microbodies

slides.narration: Lysosomes are the cell’s digestive bags, with enzymes that work in acid. Vacuoles store sap and wastes; in plants their membrane, the tonoplast, pumps ions inwards, so the sap becomes much more concentrated than the cytoplasm.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: which organelle is busy?
slides.body_md: Predict the organelle that will be most extensive in each cell.
bullets: A gland cell secreting a protein enzyme → **rough ER and Golgi apparatus**.
A cell making steroid hormones → **smooth ER**.
A white blood cell digesting engulfed bacteria → **lysosomes**.
An insect flight muscle cell → **mitochondria**, for ATP.

visual.alt: Worked table matching cell jobs to busy organelles

slides.narration: Structure follows function. A cell that exports protein is full of rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi stacks. Lipid makers have smooth reticulum. Cells that digest have many lysosomes, and very active cells have many mitochondria.

slides.heading: Mitochondria and chloroplasts
slides.body_md: Both have **two membranes**, their own **circular DNA** and **70S ribosomes**. Mitochondria (0.2 to 1.0 µm wide, 1.0 to 4.1 µm long) divide by fission.

slides.heading: Plastids
slides.body_md: Plastids occur in all plant cells and in euglenoids. Chloroplasts are mostly in the **mesophyll** of leaves: one per cell in **Chlamydomonas**, 20 to 40 per mesophyll cell; 5 to 10 µm long and 2 to 4 µm wide.

rows: Carotenoids such as carotene and xanthophylls: yellow, orange, red

visual.alt: Table of kinds of plastids

slides.narration: Plastids are named by their pigments or stores. Green chloroplasts trap light, coloured chromoplasts hold fat-soluble carotenoids, and colourless leucoplasts store starch, oils or proteins.

slides.heading: Ribosomes and the cytoskeleton
slides.body_md: Ribosomes, seen by **George Palade (1953)**, are made of **RNA and protein** and have **no membrane**. The **cytoskeleton** of microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments gives mechanical support, motility and shape.

visual.alt: Table of 80S and 70S ribosomes and their subunits

slides.narration: S stands for the Svedberg unit, a sedimentation coefficient that indirectly measures density and size. That is why a fifty S and a thirty S subunit make a seventy S ribosome: the values do not simply add up.

notes.title: Cell: The Unit of Life — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Cell theory; prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
sections.body_md:
Anything less than a complete cell does not ensure independent living, so the **cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit** of all living organisms. **Anton von Leeuwenhoek** first saw and described a live cell; **Robert Brown** later discovered the nucleus.

**Cell theory.** **Matthias Schleiden** (1838) concluded that plants are composed of different kinds of cells forming tissues. **Theodore Schwann** (1839) found that animal cells have a thin outer layer, now called the **plasma membrane**, and that the **cell wall** is unique to plant cells; he proposed that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and products of cells. Their theory did not explain how new cells form. **Rudolf Virchow** (1855) explained that cells divide and new cells form from pre-existing cells (*omnis cellula e cellula*). The modern cell theory: (i) all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells; (ii) all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

**Overview.** Cells with a membrane-bound nucleus are **eukaryotic**; those without are **prokaryotic**. Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, mitochondria, microbodies, vacuoles); ribosomes, which are not membrane-bound, occur in all cells. Animal cells have a **centrosome**. **Sizes:** Mycoplasma, the smallest cells, about **0.3 µm**; bacteria **3–5 µm**; human red blood cell about **7 µm**; the largest isolated single cell is the egg of an ostrich; nerve cells are among the longest. Shapes include disc-like, polygonal, columnar, cuboidal, thread-like and irregular.

**Plant versus animal cells.** Plant cells have a **cell wall, plastids and a large central vacuole**; animal cells have **centrioles**, absent in almost all plant cells.

key_terms.definition_md: All organisms are made of cells and cell products, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
A cell without a nuclear envelope or membrane-bound organelles.
A cell with an organised nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

sections.heading: 2. Prokaryotic cells
sections.body_md:
Prokaryotes — **bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO** (pleuro pneumonia like organisms) — are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells and multiply more rapidly. Bacteria are rod-like (**bacillus**), spherical (**coccus**), comma-shaped (**vibrio**) or spiral (**spirillum**). A cell wall surrounds the membrane in all except **mycoplasma**. There is no well-defined nucleus: the genetic material is **naked**. Besides the genomic DNA (a single circular chromosome), many bacteria have small circular **plasmids**, which confer characters such as **antibiotic resistance** and are used to monitor bacterial transformation with foreign DNA. Apart from ribosomes, there are no organelles like those of eukaryotes.

**Cell envelope.** Most prokaryotes, especially bacteria, have a chemically complex envelope of three tightly bound layers: the outer **glycocalyx**, the **cell wall** and the **plasma membrane**, acting as a single protective unit. Bacteria that take up the Gram stain are **Gram-positive**; those that do not are **Gram-negative**. The glycocalyx may be a loose sheath (**slime layer**) or thick and tough (**capsule**). The wall fixes the shape and gives strong support that stops the bacterium bursting or collapsing. The plasma membrane is selectively permeable.

**Mesosome.** An extension of the plasma membrane into the cell as vesicles, tubules and lamellae; it helps in **cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution** to daughter cells, **respiration, secretion**, and increases the membrane’s surface area and enzyme content. In cyanobacteria, **chromatophores** are membranous extensions containing pigments.

**Surface structures.** Motile bacteria have **flagella**, each with a **filament, hook and basal body**. **Pili** are elongated tubular structures of a special protein; **fimbriae** are small bristle-like fibres that help some bacteria attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues. Neither has a role in motility.

**Ribosomes and inclusions.** Ribosomes, associated with the plasma membrane, are about **15 nm by 20 nm** and are made of **50S and 30S** subunits forming **70S** ribosomes, the sites of protein synthesis. Several ribosomes on one mRNA form a **polysome (polyribosome)**. **Inclusion bodies** — phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules — store reserve material free in the cytoplasm, not bound by membranes. **Gas vacuoles** occur in blue-green, purple and green photosynthetic bacteria.

key_terms.definition_md: Outer layer of the bacterial envelope: a slime layer if loose, a capsule if thick and tough.
Infolding of the bacterial plasma membrane that aids wall formation, DNA replication and respiration.
Small circular DNA outside the bacterial chromosome, often carrying antibiotic resistance.
Several ribosomes translating one mRNA together.

sections.heading: 3. Cell membrane and cell wall
sections.body_md:
**Cell membrane.** Its detailed structure was studied after the electron microscope came into use in the 1950s. Chemical studies, especially on human **red blood cells**, showed that the membrane is mainly **lipid and protein**, the lipids (mainly **phosphoglycerides**) forming a **bilayer** with **polar heads towards the outer sides** and **hydrophobic tails towards the inside**, protecting the non-polar tails from the aqueous environment. Membranes also contain carbohydrates. The ratio of protein to lipid varies: the human red cell membrane has about **52 percent protein and 40 percent lipid**. **Peripheral proteins** lie on the surface; **integral proteins** are partly or totally buried.

The **fluid mosaic model** of **Singer and Nicolson (1972)** states that the **quasi-fluid** nature of the lipid allows **lateral movement of proteins** within the bilayer; this fluidity is important for **cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division**.

**Transport.** The membrane is **selectively permeable**. **Passive transport** needs no energy: neutral solutes cross by **simple diffusion** along the concentration gradient, and water by **osmosis**. Polar molecules cannot pass through the non-polar lipid bilayer and need **carrier proteins**. **Active transport** moves ions or molecules **against** the concentration gradient using **ATP**, as in the **sodium–potassium pump**.

**Cell wall.** A non-living rigid layer that forms the outer covering of the plasma membrane of fungi and plants. It gives **shape**, protects from **mechanical damage and infection**, helps **cell-to-cell interaction** and is a barrier to **undesirable macromolecules**. **Algal walls:** cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals such as **calcium carbonate**; **other plants:** cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins. The **primary wall** of a young cell can grow; the **secondary wall** forms on its inner side (towards the membrane) as the cell matures. The **middle lamella**, mainly **calcium pectate**, holds neighbouring cells together. **Plasmodesmata** traverse the wall and middle lamella and connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

sections.heading: 4. The endomembrane system
sections.body_md:
The **endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles** form the **endomembrane system**, because their functions are coordinated. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included.

**ER.** A network of tiny tubules dividing the intracellular space into **luminal** (inside ER) and **extra-luminal** (cytoplasm) compartments. **Rough ER (RER)** bears ribosomes, is common in cells active in **protein synthesis and secretion**, and is extensive and continuous with the outer membrane of the nucleus. **Smooth ER (SER)** is the major site of **lipid synthesis**; in animal cells lipid-like **steroidal hormones** are made in SER.

**Golgi apparatus.** **Camillo Golgi (1898)** saw densely stained reticular structures near the nucleus. It has many flat, disc-shaped sacs, **cisternae**, **0.5–1.0 µm** across, stacked in parallel and arranged concentrically near the nucleus, with a convex **cis (forming) face** and a concave **trans (maturing) face**. Its main job is **packaging** materials for intracellular targets or for secretion. Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face and move towards the trans face; proteins made on the ER are **modified** in the cisternae before release. It is an important site of **glycoprotein and glycolipid** formation.

**Lysosomes.** Membrane-bound vesicles formed by **Golgi packaging**, very rich in **hydrolytic enzymes** (hydrolases: **lipases, proteases, carbohydrases**) optimally active at **acidic pH**; they can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

**Vacuoles.** Membrane-bound spaces containing water, sap, excretory products and other materials not useful to the cell, bounded by a single membrane, the **tonoplast**. In plant cells they can occupy **up to 90 percent** of the cell volume, and the tonoplast moves ions into the vacuole **against their concentration gradient**, so their concentration is much higher than in the cytoplasm. In **Amoeba** the **contractile vacuole** carries out osmoregulation and excretion; in many protists **food vacuoles** form by engulfing food.

sections.heading: 5. Mitochondria, plastids, ribosomes, cytoskeleton, cilia, centrioles and nucleus
sections.body_md:
**Mitochondria** are not easily seen unless stained; their number depends on the cell’s physiological activity. They are sausage-shaped or cylindrical, **0.2–1.0 µm** wide (average 0.5 µm) and **1.0–4.1 µm** long. A **double membrane**: the outer membrane forms a continuous boundary; the inner membrane forms infoldings, **cristae**, that increase the surface area, around the **matrix**. Each membrane has its own enzymes. Mitochondria are the sites of **aerobic respiration** and produce **ATP** — the **power houses** of the cell. The matrix has a single **circular DNA**, a few RNA molecules, **70S ribosomes** and what is needed for protein synthesis. Mitochondria divide by **fission**.

**Plastids** occur in all plant cells and in euglenoids. **Chloroplasts** (chlorophyll and carotenoids; trap light), **chromoplasts** (fat-soluble carotenoids such as carotene and xanthophylls: yellow, orange or red) and **leucoplasts** (colourless stores: **amyloplasts** — starch, as in potato; **elaioplasts** — oils and fats; **aleuroplasts** — proteins). Chloroplasts, mainly in leaf **mesophyll**, are lens-shaped, oval, spherical, discoid or ribbon-like, **5–10 µm** long and **2–4 µm** wide; **one** per cell in *Chlamydomonas*, **20–40** per mesophyll cell. Two membranes (the inner less permeable) enclose the **stroma**, which contains **thylakoids** stacked as **grana**, joined by **stroma lamellae**; each thylakoid encloses a **lumen**. The stroma has enzymes for making **carbohydrates and proteins**, small double-stranded **circular DNA** and **70S ribosomes**. **Chlorophyll** is in the thylakoids.

**Ribosomes**, seen as dense particles by **George Palade (1953)**, are made of **RNA and protein** with **no membrane**. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are **80S** (**60S + 40S** subunits); prokaryotic are **70S** (**50S + 30S**). S is the **Svedberg unit**, a sedimentation coefficient that indirectly measures density and size.

**Cytoskeleton:** microtubules, microfilaments and intermediate filaments; mechanical support, motility and maintenance of shape.

**Cilia and flagella** are hair-like outgrowths of the membrane: cilia are small and work like oars; flagella are longer and move the cell (bacterial flagella are structurally different). The core, the **axoneme**, has **nine pairs of doublet peripheral microtubules** and a **central pair** (the **9 + 2 array**); the central tubules are joined by bridges and enclosed by a **central sheath**, linked to each peripheral doublet by a **radial spoke**; peripheral doublets are joined by **linkers**. Both arise from centriole-like **basal bodies**.

**Centrosome:** usually two cylindrical **centrioles** lying **perpendicular** to each other in amorphous **pericentriolar material**. Each has a **cartwheel** organisation of **nine evenly spaced peripheral triplet fibrils** of **tubulin**, with a central proteinaceous **hub** joined to the triplets by **radial spokes**. Centrioles form the **basal bodies** of cilia and flagella and the **spindle fibres** of animal cells during division.

**Nucleus.** Described by Robert Brown (1831); Flemming named the basic-dye-staining material **chromatin**. The **nuclear envelope** has two membranes with a **perinuclear space** of **10–50 nm**; the outer membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes; **nuclear pores** allow RNA and proteins to move both ways. The nucleoplasm contains **nucleoli** (not membrane-bound; sites of active **rRNA synthesis**; larger and more numerous in protein-making cells) and **chromatin** (DNA, basic **histones**, non-histone proteins and RNA). A human cell has about **2 m** of DNA in **46 chromosomes**. Mature red cells of many mammals and **sieve tube cells** lack a nucleus. Each chromosome has a **centromere** with disc-shaped **kinetochores**: **metacentric** (middle), **sub-metacentric** (nearer one end), **acrocentric** (close to one end; one extremely short arm), **telocentric** (terminal). Some chromosomes have a non-staining **secondary constriction** that gives a small fragment called the **satellite**.

**Microbodies:** minute membrane-bound vesicles containing various enzymes, in plant and animal cells.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Crediting Schleiden and Schwann with "cells from pre-existing cells" (that was Virchow).
- Adding S values: 50S and 30S make 70S, not 80S.
- Placing mitochondria or chloroplasts in the endomembrane system.
- Reversing the Golgi faces (enter at cis, leave at trans).
- Calling a secondary wall the outer layer (it forms on the inner side of the primary wall).
- Describing the axoneme as 9 triplets (that is the centriole) or the centriole as 9 + 2.
- Saying ribosomes are bounded by a membrane.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name an organelle, a scientist, a plastid, a chromosome type or a transport process.
- 2–3-mark answers: cell theory; prokaryote versus eukaryote; fluid mosaic model; transport classification; RER versus SER; plastid types; chromosome types.
- 5-mark answers: prokaryotic cell; membrane and wall; endomembrane system; mitochondria and chloroplasts compared; nucleus and chromosomes.
- Case-based items: a bacterial culture, red cell membranes, a protein-tracking experiment or leaf and root plastids, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Schleiden and Schwann’s cell theory did not explain how new cells form. Who supplied this missing idea, and what was it?

options.text_md: Rudolf Virchow: all cells arise from pre-existing cells
Robert Brown: every cell has a nucleus
Anton von Leeuwenhoek: cells can be seen alive
Theodore Schwann: plant cells have a cell wall

questions.solution_md: Virchow (1855) explained that cells divide and new cells form from pre-existing cells, omnis cellula e cellula — option (a).

questions.stem_md: From his study of animal cells, Theodore Schwann reported that

options.text_md: cells have a thin outer layer, now called the plasma membrane, and the cell wall is a feature of plant cells
all cells arise from pre-existing cells
the nucleus is the control centre of the cell
ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis

questions.solution_md: Schwann (1839) reported the thin outer layer of animal cells and concluded that the cell wall is unique to plant cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The smallest cells known, only about 0.3 µm in length, belong to
questions.solution_md: Mycoplasma cells are about 0.3 µm long; bacteria are 3–5 µm and human red cells about 7 µm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A bacterium survives an antibiotic that kills its neighbours, and it can pass this resistance to other bacteria. The resistance gene is most likely on

options.text_md: a plasmid, a small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA

questions.solution_md: Plasmids give bacteria characters such as antibiotic resistance — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is NOT a function of the mesosome of a bacterium?

options.text_md: Helping in DNA replication and its distribution to daughter cells
Increasing the surface area and enzyme content of the plasma membrane

questions.solution_md: Mesosomes help in wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration and secretion, and enlarge the membrane surface; bacteria have no grana — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Bacteria in a fast mountain stream stay attached to the rocks instead of being washed away. Which surface structures help them?
questions.solution_md: Fimbriae, small bristle-like fibres, help some bacteria attach to rocks in streams and to host tissues — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A prokaryotic ribosome is formed of

options.text_md: a 60S and a 40S subunit, making an 80S ribosome
a 50S and a 30S subunit, making an 80S ribosome
a 50S and a 30S subunit, making a 70S ribosome
a single 70S unit with no subunits

questions.solution_md: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S, with 50S and 30S subunits — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A cyanobacterium stores phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules and glycogen granules free in its cytoplasm. These are

options.text_md: inclusion bodies, not bounded by any membrane

questions.solution_md: Reserve materials stored free in the cytoplasm of prokaryotes are inclusion bodies — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A cell has a cell wall, ribosomes and a circular DNA lying free in the cytoplasm, but no nuclear envelope, mitochondria or Golgi apparatus. It is most likely
questions.solution_md: No nuclear envelope and no membrane-bound organelles mark a prokaryote — option (d).

questions.stem_md: An unknown eukaryotic cell has centrioles but no cell wall, no plastids and no large central vacuole. It is most likely
questions.solution_md: Animal cells have centrioles and lack the wall, plastids and large central vacuole of plant cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mycoplasma keeps a fixed shape because it has a rigid cell wall.

**Reason (R):** Mycoplasma is a prokaryote.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: Mycoplasma is the prokaryote without a cell wall; R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Several ribosomes attached to a single mRNA form a chain called a polyribosome or ______.
questions.solution_md: Polysome.

questions.stem_md: A human red blood cell is about 7 µm across, and a Mycoplasma cell about 0.3 µm. How many times wider is the red blood cell? (One decimal place.)
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{7}{0.3} \approx 23.3$ times.

questions.stem_md: State the modern cell theory and name the scientist whose idea completed it.

answer.model_answer_md: The cell theory states that (i) **all living organisms are composed of cells and products of cells**, and (ii) **all cells arise from pre-existing cells**. Schleiden and Schwann proposed the first part; **Rudolf Virchow** (1855) added the second.

questions.solution_md: Two statements and Virchow.

marking_scheme.step: Virchow added cells from pre-existing cells

questions.stem_md: Name the three layers of the bacterial cell envelope, and distinguish a slime layer from a capsule.

answer.model_answer_md: From outside inwards the envelope has the **glycocalyx**, the **cell wall** and the **plasma membrane**, acting together as one protective unit. A **slime layer** is a **loose sheath** of glycocalyx; a **capsule** is a **thick and tough** glycocalyx.

questions.solution_md: Three layers; slime layer vs capsule.

marking_scheme.step: Slime layer loose; capsule thick and tough

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Nucleus:** prokaryotes have **no nuclear envelope**; the genetic material is naked. Eukaryotes have an organised nucleus with a **nuclear envelope**.
2. **Organelles:** prokaryotes have **no membrane-bound organelles** (only ribosomes); eukaryotes have ER, Golgi, mitochondria and others.
3. **Ribosomes:** prokaryotes have **70S** ribosomes; eukaryotic cytoplasm has **80S** ribosomes. Prokaryotes are also generally **smaller** and multiply faster.

questions.solution_md: Nucleus, organelles, ribosomes.

questions.stem_md: Two eukaryotic cells are seen under a microscope: cell X has a thick rigid boundary outside its membrane and a large central vacuole, and cell Y has neither. Identify them and give three structural differences that support your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
**X is a plant cell** and **Y is an animal cell**.
1. Plant cells have a **cell wall** outside the plasma membrane; animal cells do not.
2. Plant cells have **plastids** such as chloroplasts; animal cells lack them.
3. Plant cells have a **large central vacuole**, while animal cells have small or no vacuoles; animal cells have **centrioles**, absent in almost all plant cells.

questions.solution_md: Plant X, animal Y; wall, plastids, vacuole and centrioles.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of a typical prokaryotic cell, including its cell envelope, membrane extensions, surface structures, genetic material, ribosomes and inclusion bodies.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma and PPLO) are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells and multiply faster. Bacteria may be rods (bacillus), spheres (coccus), commas (vibrio) or spirals (spirillum).

**Cell envelope.** Most have a chemically complex envelope of three tightly bound layers: an outer **glycocalyx** (a loose **slime layer** or a thick, tough **capsule**), a **cell wall** that fixes the shape and prevents bursting or collapse, and a selectively permeable **plasma membrane**. Differences in the envelope underlie the **Gram-positive** and **Gram-negative** reaction. Mycoplasma has no wall.

**Membrane extensions.** The **mesosome**, an infolding of the plasma membrane as vesicles, tubules and lamellae, helps in wall formation, DNA replication and distribution, respiration and secretion, and increases membrane area. Cyanobacteria have pigment-containing **chromatophores**.

**Surface structures.** Motile bacteria have **flagella**, each with a filament, hook and basal body. **Pili** are tubular protein structures, and **fimbriae** are bristle-like fibres that help attachment; neither aids motility.

**Genetic material.** There is no nuclear envelope; the genomic DNA, a single circular chromosome, lies naked. Small circular **plasmids** carry genes such as antibiotic resistance.

**Ribosomes and inclusions.** **70S ribosomes** (50S + 30S), about 15 nm by 20 nm, are associated with the membrane and may form **polysomes** on an mRNA. **Inclusion bodies**, free of membranes, store phosphate, cyanophycean and glycogen granules; some photosynthetic bacteria have **gas vacuoles**.

questions.solution_md: Envelope, mesosome, appendages, DNA, ribosomes, inclusions.

marking_scheme.step: Envelope layers, slime layer and capsule

options.text_md: hydrophobic tails towards both outer surfaces
polar heads towards the outer sides and hydrophobic tails towards the inner part
polar heads all towards the cytoplasm only
tails and heads mixed at random

questions.solution_md: The non-polar tails are protected from the aqueous surroundings inside the bilayer — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which group of processes depends on the fluid nature of the plasma membrane?

options.text_md: Cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division
Replication of DNA in the nucleus only
Absorption of light by chlorophyll only
Synthesis of rRNA in the nucleolus only

questions.solution_md: Membrane fluidity is needed for growth, junctions, secretion, endocytosis and division — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Red blood cells placed in distilled water swell and burst. Which process causes this?

options.text_md: Active transport of salts out of the cells
Osmosis: water moves into the cells across the membrane
Movement of membrane proteins to one side
Digestion of the membrane by lysosomes

questions.solution_md: Water diffuses into the cells by osmosis, down its own concentration gradient — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A cell keeps pumping sodium ions out although their concentration is already higher outside. This movement

options.text_md: is simple diffusion and needs no energy
happens only through the lipid tails without proteins
is active transport that uses energy from ATP

questions.solution_md: Moving ions against the concentration gradient requires ATP, as in the sodium–potassium pump — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why do polar molecules need a carrier protein to cross the plasma membrane?

options.text_md: They are always larger than the membrane
They move only against the gradient
They cannot pass through the non-polar lipid bilayer

questions.solution_md: The hydrophobic interior of the bilayer blocks polar molecules, so they need carriers — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Neighbouring plant cells are held together by the middle lamella, which is made mainly of
questions.solution_md: The middle lamella is a layer mainly of calcium pectate — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which set of substances makes up the cell walls of algae?

options.text_md: Cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals such as calcium carbonate

questions.solution_md: Algal walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate; other plants have cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A plant virus moves from one leaf cell to the next without ever passing into the space outside the cells. Which structures could it use?

options.text_md: Plasmodesmata, which connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells

questions.solution_md: Plasmodesmata cross the wall and middle lamella and connect neighbouring cytoplasms — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The membrane of a human red blood cell is about 40 percent lipid by mass. What mass of lipid would be present in 8 mg of such membrane?
State four functions of the plant cell wall.

answer.model_answer_md: The cell wall is a **non-living rigid** layer that (i) **gives shape** to the cell, (ii) **protects** it from **mechanical damage and infection**, (iii) helps in **cell-to-cell interaction**, and (iv) acts as a **barrier to undesirable macromolecules**.

questions.solution_md: Four functions.

questions.stem_md: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane.

answer.model_answer_md: Proposed by **Singer and Nicolson (1972)**, the model describes the membrane as a **lipid bilayer**, mainly of **phosphoglycerides**, with **polar heads** facing outwards and **hydrophobic tails** inwards. **Proteins** are a mosaic within it: **integral proteins** are partly or totally buried, and **peripheral proteins** lie on the surface; carbohydrates are also present. The lipid is **quasi-fluid**, so **proteins can move laterally**; this fluidity is needed for growth, junctions, secretion, endocytosis and division.

questions.solution_md: Bilayer, proteins, fluidity.

questions.stem_md: Classify each movement as simple diffusion, osmosis or active transport, with a reason: (i) oxygen entering a cell where its concentration is low; (ii) water entering a root hair cell with a concentrated sap; (iii) a plant cell taking up ions into its vacuole against their gradient.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Simple diffusion**: oxygen moves **down its concentration gradient** without energy (passive).

(ii) **Osmosis**: **water** moves across the membrane towards the more concentrated sap, also passively.

(iii) **Active transport**: ions move **against the concentration gradient**, which needs energy from **ATP**; the tonoplast carries out such transport.

questions.solution_md: Diffusion, osmosis, active transport.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the plasma membrane according to the fluid mosaic model and explain how substances move across it. Add a short account of the plant cell wall.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Composition.** Chemical studies, especially on human red blood cells, showed that the membrane is mainly **lipid and protein**, with some carbohydrate; the red cell membrane has about **52 percent protein and 40 percent lipid**. The lipids, mainly **phosphoglycerides**, form a **bilayer**, with **polar heads** towards the outer sides and **hydrophobic tails** inside.

**Fluid mosaic model.** Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed that the **quasi-fluid** lipid lets **proteins move laterally** within the bilayer. **Integral proteins** are partly or totally buried; **peripheral proteins** lie on the surface. Fluidity is important for cell growth, intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis and cell division.

**Transport.** The membrane is **selectively permeable**. In **passive transport** substances move along the concentration gradient without energy: neutral solutes by **simple diffusion**, and water by **osmosis**. Polar molecules cannot pass the non-polar bilayer and need **carrier proteins**. In **active transport**, molecules move **against** the gradient using **ATP**, as in the **sodium–potassium pump**.

**Cell wall.** Plant and fungal cells have a non-living rigid wall outside the membrane that gives shape, protects against mechanical damage and infection, aids cell-to-cell interaction and blocks undesirable macromolecules. Algal walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans and calcium carbonate; other plants have cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins. A **primary wall** grows in young cells; a **secondary wall** forms on its inner side. The **middle lamella** of calcium pectate glues neighbours together, and **plasmodesmata** connect their cytoplasm.

questions.solution_md: Model, transport, wall.

questions.stem_md: Which organelle is NOT part of the endomembrane system?

questions.stem_md: What is the endomembrane system? Describe the structure and functions of its components.

answer.model_answer_md:
Many membranous organelles work in a **coordinated** way and are grouped as the **endomembrane system**: the **endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles**. Mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded because their functions are not coordinated with these.

**Endoplasmic reticulum.** A network of tiny tubules that divides the cell into a **luminal** and an **extra-luminal** compartment. **Rough ER** bears ribosomes, is continuous with the outer nuclear membrane and is extensive in cells that make and secrete proteins. **Smooth ER** is the main site of **lipid synthesis**; in animal cells it makes **steroidal hormones**.

**Golgi apparatus.** Described by Camillo Golgi (1898), it is a stack of flat, disc-shaped **cisternae** (0.5–1.0 µm across) near the nucleus, with a convex **cis (forming) face** and a concave **trans (maturing) face**. Vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face; proteins are modified and **packaged**, and leave from the trans face for secretion or for use inside the cell. It is the main site of **glycoprotein and glycolipid** formation.

**Lysosomes.** Membrane-bound vesicles formed by Golgi packaging, rich in **hydrolytic enzymes** (lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) active at **acidic pH**; they can digest carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.

**Vacuoles.** Membrane-bound spaces holding water, sap and excretory products, bounded by the **tonoplast**. In plants they may fill **up to 90 percent** of the cell, and the tonoplast moves ions in against their gradient. **Contractile vacuoles** of Amoeba osmoregulate; **food vacuoles** form when protists engulf food.

questions.solution_md: Definition; ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles.

questions.stem_md: Compare the structure and functions of mitochondria and chloroplasts, and explain which shared features suggest that both can make some of their own proteins and multiply within the cell.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Mitochondria.** Sausage-shaped or cylindrical, about 0.2–1.0 µm wide and 1.0–4.1 µm long, their number depends on the cell’s activity. Each has **two membranes**: a smooth outer membrane and an inner membrane folded into **cristae**, which increase the surface area. The **matrix** inside holds enzymes of aerobic respiration, a **single circular DNA**, a few RNA molecules and **70S ribosomes**. They are the sites of **aerobic respiration** and make **ATP**, so they are called the power houses of the cell.

**Chloroplasts.** Lens-shaped or oval, about 5–10 µm long and 2–4 µm wide, mainly in the mesophyll (20–40 per cell; one in Chlamydomonas). They have **two membranes**, the inner less permeable. Inside, the **stroma** holds flattened **thylakoids** stacked into **grana**, joined by **stroma lamellae**; chlorophyll lies in the thylakoids. The stroma contains enzymes for making **carbohydrates and proteins**, **circular DNA** and **70S ribosomes**. They **trap light energy** for photosynthesis.

**Shared features.** Both are **double-membrane** organelles outside the endomembrane system. Both have their **own circular DNA** and **70S ribosomes**, smaller than the 80S ribosomes of the cytoplasm, plus the components for protein synthesis; so each can make some of its own proteins. Mitochondria are known to **divide by fission**. These features show that both organelles are partly independent of the nucleus in their growth and multiplication, although most of their proteins are still coded by nuclear genes.

questions.solution_md: Structure, function, shared features, reasoning.

questions.stem_md: Describe the structure of the interphase nucleus and of chromosomes.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Discovery.** Robert Brown described the nucleus in 1831; Flemming named the material that takes up basic dyes **chromatin**.

**Nuclear envelope.** Two parallel membranes separated by a **perinuclear space** of 10–50 nm form a barrier between nucleus and cytoplasm. The **outer membrane** is continuous with the **ER** and bears ribosomes. At many places the two membranes fuse to form **nuclear pores**, through which **RNA and proteins** move in both directions.

**Contents.** The **nucleoplasm** holds one or more spherical **nucleoli**, not bounded by membranes, which are sites of active **ribosomal RNA** synthesis; cells making much protein have larger, more numerous nucleoli. **Chromatin**, a loose network of nucleoprotein fibres, contains **DNA**, basic **histone** proteins, non-histone proteins and RNA. A human cell has about **two metres** of DNA in **46 chromosomes**. Usually there is one nucleus per cell, but mature mammalian red cells and sieve tube cells have none.

**Chromosomes.** During division chromatin condenses into chromosomes. Each has a **primary constriction**, the **centromere**, with disc-shaped **kinetochores**. By centromere position they are **metacentric** (middle, equal arms), **sub-metacentric** (nearer one end), **acrocentric** (close to one end, one extremely short arm) and **telocentric** (terminal). Some chromosomes have a non-staining **secondary constriction** that cuts off a small **satellite**.

questions.solution_md: Envelope, nucleolus, chromatin, chromosomes.
